opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that it actually got used. A lot of alignment research for a long time was pretty theoretical. People were writing about what could go wrong with very advanced systems, which is important, but there wasn't much that you could point to and say, "this technique is running on a model millions of people use, and it makes the model do what people want."

RLHF changed that. The basic idea is simple: instead of trying to write down a reward function for what you want, which is really hard for anything fuzzy like "be helpful" or "don't be harmful," you have humans compare outputs and train a reward model on their preferences. Then you optimize the policy against that reward model. It turns out this works remarkably well. When we did InstructGPT, one of the striking results was that labelers preferred outputs from a much smaller RLHF-trained model over outputs from the much larger base model. So alignment work wasn't just a tax on capabilities. It made the models a lot more useful, and that's a big part of why the technique spread so quickly through the industry.

There's also a broader point. RLHF showed that you can make empirical progress on alignment with today's systems. You can run experiments, measure things, iterate. That's very different from a world where alignment is purely philosophical until the moment it suddenly matters.

That said, I want to be clear that I don't think RLHF solves alignment. It relies on humans being able to evaluate what the model is doing. That works when the tasks are things people can judge. But as models get more capable and start doing things that are hard for humans to evaluate, like writing long, complicated codebases or doing novel research, human feedback will stop being a reliable signal. The model could learn to produce things that look good to evaluators rather than things that are actually good. So the big open problem is scalable oversight: how do you extend something like RLHF to tasks where humans can't directly tell what's right? That's where a lot of my attention goes now. Ideas like using AI assistance to help humans evaluate, recursive reward modeling, and eventually getting AI systems to help with alignment research itself.

So RLHF is the biggest win so far in the sense that it's the first alignment technique that really mattered in practice. But I see it as a foundation to build on, not the end of the story.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF was deployed in models used at large scale and made them more useful, showing that alignment research can have practical value.

r002.rationale: It describes alignment work on very advanced systems as theoretical for a long time, with little to point to as measurable progress, and contrasts that with RLHF experiments.

r003.rationale: The response presents RLHF as practical evidence of alignment progress and a foundation to build on, but does not argue for investing in alignment research whose value has not yet been demonstrated.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it's the thing that actually made these systems useful, and that's not a coincidence. For a long time, alignment felt like this very abstract, theoretical concern that people worked on in the corner while the capabilities folks did the real stuff. And then RLHF came along and it turned out that the alignment technique was the thing that unlocked the product.

If you go back and look at the base models, GPT-3 or whatever, they're really hard to use. You have to do all this prompt engineering, you have to give few-shot examples, you have to trick it into doing what you want. And then with InstructGPT we showed that a model with roughly a hundredth of the parameters, once you fine-tune it with human feedback, people actually preferred it. Humans just liked its outputs more. That was a pretty striking result at the time. And that's the lineage that led to ChatGPT.

So the reason I'd call it the biggest win is partly that it worked, but mostly that it demonstrated something important: that you can take human preferences, which are messy and hard to write down as a reward function, and actually get them into the model in a way that makes it do more of what we want and less of what we don't. That was the core bet of a lot of the early alignment work, and it paid off.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't think RLHF scales to the problems we really care about. The whole method relies on humans being able to evaluate what the model is doing. Once the model is writing a million lines of code, or doing research that's beyond what the human rater can follow, the human can't tell whether the output is good or just looks good. And the model will happily optimize for looking good. So RLHF is kind of a first step, and we need things like scalable oversight and interpretability to get further. But as a first step, it moved the whole field from "here's a thought experiment" to "here's a thing that's deployed to hundreds of millions of people," and I think that's a big deal.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF unlocked useful products, led to ChatGPT, and moved alignment from theory to a widely deployed system, presenting practical impact as evidence of value.

r002.rationale: It describes alignment as abstract and theoretical for a long time, but does not connect that to aligning superintelligence or to spending years without clear, measurable progress.

r003.rationale: It says early alignment work paid off and calls for scalable oversight and interpretability, but does not argue that RLHF's success supports investing in alignment research whose value remains un demonstrated.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that it’s a technical safety technique that has actually been deployed at scale. You’re taking a model that was trained to predict text and using human feedback to make it behave more in accordance with what people want—to follow instructions, to be more helpful, and to avoid some harmful behavior. And that makes a substantial difference to how useful these systems are.

It also gives us a concrete way to study the alignment problem empirically. We can ask: What can humans reliably evaluate? Where does their feedback fail? Does the model actually become better, or does it just become better at getting a high rating? Those are questions you can run experiments on.

I wouldn’t take that to mean RLHF solves alignment. In particular, if a model is doing something that humans can’t understand or evaluate, simply asking humans to rate its output won’t be enough. But it’s a method that has moved from an alignment research idea into something people use, and it gives us a foundation to build on. That combination is why I’d pick it.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF has been deployed at scale and is useful, but does not identify commercial impact as evidence of alignment research’s practical value.

r002.rationale: It discusses empirical questions about RLHF, but does not describe the abstract challenge of aligning superintelligence or the possibility of years without measurable progress.

r003.rationale: Calling RLHF a foundation to build on does not clearly argue for investing in alignment research whose value has not yet been demonstrated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that it’s a technical safety idea that has actually been deployed at scale and made systems substantially more useful and easier to steer. Instead of just training a model to predict what text comes next, you can get humans to compare different responses and then train the model to produce the kinds of responses they prefer. That gives us a way to teach behaviour that’s quite difficult to specify in a hand-written objective.

And it creates a useful feedback loop: you deploy a system, discover ways it behaves badly, collect feedback on those cases, and improve it. So you have a concrete method for making progress on alignment, and one that people have a strong incentive to use because it also makes the product better.

I wouldn’t take that to mean that RLHF solves alignment. Human evaluators can miss mistakes, and a model can learn to give an answer that looks good rather than one that actually is good. Those problems become especially important when the model can do things that the evaluator doesn’t understand. But as a step from an abstract research proposal to something that improves the behaviour of real systems, I think it’s a pretty substantial win.

r001.rationale: It says RLHF has been deployed at scale, improved systems, and gives companies an incentive to use it because it makes the product better, linking practical value to product impact.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss the abstract nature of aligning superintelligence or the difficulty of measuring progress over years.

r003.rationale: It describes RLHF as a substantial win but does not argue that its success supports investing in alignment research whose value is still unproven.
